title: Lesson 66: Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architecture: DevOps at Enterprise Scale
description: How enterprise teams take a build from a developer's machine to a monitored, released production system. Source control and branching strategy, continuous integration and continuous delivery, environment promotion through the sandbox chain, and the observability that tells you a release is actually working.

questions.question: What value does continuous integration add to a Salesforce team's delivery lifecycle?
options: It replaces the need for a branching strategy entirely by merging all work directly into production on a fixed schedule every night.
It merges every change into a shared main line often and validates each merge, so integration problems surface early and cheaply.
It removes the need for source control because every change is automatically tested before it can reach the production org.
It ships every change straight to production on each merge without any separate validation or review step.
questions.explanation: Continuous integration validates every merge to the shared main line, so a change that breaks the build is caught the day it is merged rather than the week before release, when the fix is far more expensive.

questions.question: An org deploys a release successfully. What does it take to know the change is actually working in production?
options: Waiting for the next release, because only the following version can reveal whether the prior one actually held up in front of real users.
Completing the deployment, because a successful deploy proves the change behaves correctly in production.
Observing the release through logs, metrics, and traces, because a deployment is not the same as a working system.
Validating the change set in a sandbox, because pre-production testing is the final and definitive check.
questions.explanation: A deployment moves metadata, a release makes it visible, and a working system is known only by watching evidence in production; observability is what closes the loop that a successful deployment leaves open.

questions.question: Why is a branching strategy best treated as a governance decision rather than a tooling detail?
options: The branching strategy is a governance decision that sets who may merge, how often, and what must be true first.
The branching strategy is a tooling detail that only affects where files are physically stored and how quickly they can be checked out.
The branching strategy matters only for teams that have never adopted continuous integration or automated testing.
The branching strategy can safely be deferred until the team is already under pressure to ship a release.
questions.explanation: The branching strategy decides who can merge, how often, and what has to be true before a merge is allowed; without that decision, teams accumulate merge conflicts that surface at the worst possible moment, release time.
